analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to disclose the funding and conflicts behind studies they submit to federal regulators, and makes rulemaking more transparent to the public.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: after being referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in July 2024 with 10 cosponsors, it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agencies write the detailed rules that carry out laws on everything from air pollution to drug safety, and corporations weigh in heavily on those rules, often by submitting research they paid for. This bill would require anyone submitting a scientific, economic, or technical study to a rulemaking to disclose who funded it, who was allowed to review or edit it, and any financial ties to parties affected by the rule. Public companies that knowingly submit false information would face civil penalties starting at $250,000. It would also require agencies to publicly disclose what changed in a rule after White House review, explain why any rule was withdrawn, respond to petitions with 100,000 signatures, create an Office of the Public Advocate to help ordinary people participate in rulemaking, and restore court deference to agencies' reading of the laws they administer.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who depend on public health, safety, consumer, environmental, and financial rules. Regulators would be able to see and disclose when the research in their dockets was paid for by the companies being regulated, and the public would see it too. Workers, consumers, and communities affected by rules would get help participating through a new public advocate office, faster agency response to large petitions, and plain-language notice of proposed rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who rely on public-health, safety, and consumer rules

how_it_helps.text: Anyone submitting a study to a rulemaking that they funded directly or indirectly must disclose the amount and source of the funding, any entity allowed to review or revise the study, and any financial relationship between the researcher and anyone affected by the rule [S2].

If at least 10% of a submitted study's funding comes from an entity the agency regulates, or a regulated entity exercises editorial control over it, the agency must disclose that conflict publicly on its website, its docket, and in the Federal Register [S2].

Public companies that knowingly submit materially false information in rulemaking would face civil penalties of at least $250,000 for a first violation and at least $1 million for repeat violations, and false submissions could be excluded from the record permanently [S2].

Agencies would have to publish the substance of any changes made to a rule after White House regulatory review and state whether the changes came from the White House office, another agency, or other federal officials — and explain publicly why any rule was withdrawn [S2].

A new Office of the Public Advocate inside the budget office would help individuals and communities that historically have not participated in rulemaking take part, and agencies would have to respond in writing to any petition signed by more than 100,000 people [S2].

Courts would be directed to defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation of a statute the agency administers, and could not require a rule to pass a cost-benefit test unless a statute demands one — restoring deference courts had applied for decades before the Supreme Court ended it in 2024 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Regulated industries — companies in pharmaceuticals, chemicals, energy, finance, and other sectors that routinely submit their own research and comments during rulemaking. They would have to disclose funding and financial ties behind their studies, could see conflicted studies flagged publicly, and as public companies would face six-figure penalties for false submissions. Industry-funded consultants and trade associations that produce such research would also bear new disclosure obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Regulated industries and their funded researchers

drawbacks.text: Disclosure of unpublished studies and their funders could expose commercially confidential research information, a burden that falls on any company or organization filing comments — and drafting errors could be penalized harshly, starting at $250,000 for a public company's knowing false statement [S2].

Requiring the White House regulatory office to finish its review of a significant rule in 60 days, with only one 60-day extension, could rush the review that agencies and affected parties use to fix technical problems before rules are finalized [S2].

Narrowing negotiated rulemaking — the process where agencies convene affected stakeholders to draft rules by consensus — to only government participants would cut businesses and public interest groups out of those committees, on the theory that industry had captured them [S2].

Requiring courts to defer to agencies' interpretations and barring cost-benefit challenges would make agency rules harder to challenge in court, which reduces a check on agency overreach even as it protects rules from industry lawsuits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is transparency for disclosure burden. Requiring researchers to name who paid for and edited the studies agencies rely on addresses a real problem: regulated industries dominate rulemaking dockets with funded research that can look independent. The bill's strongest pieces are the conflict disclosures, the false-statement penalties, and the public reporting of White House edits and withdrawn rules. Its weakest are procedural boilerplate and a hard 60-day White House review clock that could degrade review quality. On balance, the disclosure and public-participation benefits for everyday people outweigh the compliance costs, which fall mainly on the industries being regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was filed, and the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 23, 2024, joined by 10 original cosponsors — nine Senate Democrats and one Independent [S1][S2][S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the full Senate never voted on it [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without coming to a vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and industry groups that submit their own funded research during federal rulemaking are better off — they keep filing studies without having to disclose who funded them, who edited them, or their financial ties, and they avoid new penalties for false submissions. Officials and interest groups that benefit from limited public participation in rulemaking also keep the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated industries and their funded researchers

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Corporate Capture Act and led its case for disclosing industry funding behind studies submitted to regulators.

for.name: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Blumenthal, Merkley, Hirono, Lujan, Van Hollen, Markey, Wyden, Booker, Welch).

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Senate committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Gary Peters, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no partisan split was recorded; all 10 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and no Republican signed on [S3].

industries.industry: Regulated corporations (pharmaceutical, chemical, energy, financial, and other companies that file rulemaking comments)
industries.note: These companies dominate federal rulemaking dockets with their own research and comments. The bill would force them to disclose funding, reviewers, and financial ties behind submitted studies, flag studies with 10% or more regulated-entity funding as conflicts, and expose public companies to penalties starting at $250,000 for knowing false submissions [S2].

industries.industry: Industry-funded consultants, think tanks, and trade associations
industries.note: Groups that produce or commission research for clients affected by rules would face the same disclosure requirements, and their work could be publicly flagged as conflicted or excluded from consideration if disclosures were missing [S2].

industries.industry: Businesses participating in negotiated rulemaking committees
industries.note: The bill would limit negotiated rulemaking — committees that draft rules by consensus — to representatives of federal, state, local, and tribal governments, removing business and public-interest stakeholders from those committees on the theory that well-funded interests had come to dominate them [S2].
